Abstract
In recent years, in the context of the rapid development of quantum computing
technology, quantum attack methods such as Shor’s algorithm pose a serious threat
to the traditional public key encryption system based on number-theoretic puzzles.
Using the characteristics of quantum bits, this paper proposes a quantum grey-scale
image encryption method based on alternating quantum random walk. Firstly, the
quantum representation model is used to transform the image into a quantum state,
and then the quantum key is generated by the alternating quantum random walk
algorithm, and combined with the quantum gate operation for encrypting the
grey-scale image data, which not only inherits the advantage of the anti-attack of the
quantum computation, but also, through the quantum parallelism and the
non-clonability, which solves the security and eﬃciency bottleneck of traditional
image encryption in the quantum era and signiﬁcantly improves the security of
grey-scale image encryption. The algorithm proposed in this paper has been veriﬁed
by simulation experiments, and the experimental results show that the method is
excellent in encryption and decryption eﬀects, and for the encrypted image, a
number of performance analyses have been carried out, and the analysis results show
that the proposed encryption method has a high degree of security, and it can
eﬀectively resist the statistical attack, noise attack, etc., and the distribution of the
histogram of encrypted image is more uniform, the pixel correlation analysis is close
to 1, and the information entropy is close to 7.999.

quantum computation, and the strong computational capabilities of quantum computers

Quantum random walk (QRW) is an extension of classical random walk (CRW) in the
framework of quantum mechanics [12–14]. By virtue of its unique quantum superposition
and interference properties, it demonstrates a great potential for application in a variety of
ﬁelds such as quantum computing, quantum simulation, quantum algorithms, and quan-
tum information processing. The concept of quantum random walk was ﬁrst proposed by
Aharonov et al. in 1993 [15], Aharonov proposed the basic theory of quantum random
walk and revealed that quantum particles can be superimposed on multiple paths. This
discovery provided a new idea for the ﬁeld of quantum algorithms and quantum informa-
tion and promoted the research on quantum random walk. Despite the groundbreaking
signiﬁcance of this theory, it was not until the beginning of the 21st century that quan-
tum random walk really entered the systematic research stage. In 2001, Watrous et al.
proposed the framework of discrete-time quantum random walk (DTQW) [16], which
greatly promoted the research on quantum random walk, and DTQW controls the par-
ticle motion through the introduction of the “quantum coin” operation to control the di-
rection of particle motion, and this operation changes the quantum state of the particle at
each step, thus making the walking process show typical quantum behaviour. This theory
not only deepens the fundamental theory of quantum random walk, but also reveals its
potential application value in quantum algorithms. Through quantum superposition and
interference [17–19], quantum walks are able to traverse a larger space in a ﬁnite time,
and thus show higher eﬃciency in speciﬁc applications. This discovery provides a new
solution to the search problem in quantum computation, and plays an important role in
promoting the research of applications such as quantum simulation and quantum search
algorithms. In contrast to the discrete-time quantum random walk, the continuous-time
quantum random walk (CTQW), as another quantum walk model, was proposed by Farhi
and Gutmann in 1998 [20], CTQW directly uses Hamiltonian quantum evolution to de-
scribe the motion of particles without the need to introduce the “quantum coin” operation.
The proposed model expands the application scope of quantum walks in quantum physics,
quantum computation and quantum simulation, and is of great signiﬁcance in quantum
information science.

2 Theoretical foundations
2.1 Alternating quantum random walk
The quantum random walk is a quantum-mechanical extension of the classical random
walk, ﬁrst proposed by Aharonov et al. in 1993. In a classical random walk, a particle can
occupy only a single spatial position in discrete time steps, and the state at each moment is
jointly determined by the state at the previous moment and a random factor. The quantum
random walk, on the other hand, allows particles to occupy multiple positions in a super-
position of states at the same time by introducing quantum superposition of states. This

Page 4 of 20
quantum superposition eﬀect allows the particles to “exist” in multiple positions simulta-
neously, and the distribution of their positions over time exhibits a diﬀusive behaviour that
is completely diﬀerent from that of the classical random walk. This diﬀusion behaviour is
in most cases more rapid than the classical diﬀusion, and can exhibit more complex and
ﬁne propagation properties through quantum interference. In the quantum random walk
model, the motion of the particle is not only dependent on its spatial location, but is also
coupled with an additional coin degree of freedom. This coin degree of freedom is not a
coin in the traditional sense, but represents the “direction choice” of the particle at each
time step, and describes the possible directions of the particle’s motion in space through
quantum superposition states. The coin degree of freedom and the position degree of
freedom together constitute a composite system of quantum random walk, and its math-
ematical description is realized through composite Hilbert space. Assume that the total
Hilbert space of the system is H = Hc ⊗Hp, where Hc is the Hilbert space of the coin’s
degrees of freedom, containing the two eigenstates |0⟩and |1⟩, and Hp is the degree of
freedom describing the position of the particle.
The core of the quantum random walk lies in the way the particle evolves at each evo-
lutionary step, with its spatial position determined by the coin state. When the coin state
is |0⟩, the positional state of the particle moves to the right, i.e., evolves from position |n⟩
to position |n + 1⟩; when the coin state is |1⟩, the positional state of the particle moves to
the left, i.e., evolves from position |n⟩evolves to position |n – 1⟩. The whole evolution of
the quantum random walk is realised iteratively by applying alternately the coin operator
ˆC to and the shift operator S to the dynamics of the quantum walk. The coin operator and
the shift operator ﬁt into the evolution operator ˆU, which can be expressed as:

3 Proposed encryption method
This method achieves double enhancement through the quantum transformation of the
algorithm kernel, providing a native-level protection barrier against quantum computing
attacks. Figure 4 shows the ﬂowchart of the encryption method proposed in this paper,
and Fig. 5 is the image encryption algorithm diagram.
Step 1: Image preprocessing. First, preprocess the image, for 2N × 2N an image of size,
divide it into blocks of size 2n × 2n, so the total number of blocks is 2(N+N)–(n+n). After
block division, each image block can be converted to a quantum state independently, and
quantum walk and encryption operations can be performed in parallel, which signiﬁcantly
improves processing eﬃciency. If the block processing is not performed, but the complete
image is selected for the second step, it is easy to be limited by hardware resources, for
example, a 1024 × 1024 grayscale image is directly converted into a quantum state, which
requires 10 + 10 + 8 = 28 quantum bits, and subsequent encryption operations require
more quantum bits, so block processing is selected.
Step 2: Transform the quantum state. For each image block of size after segmentation
2n × 2n, use the NEQR model to transform it into a quantum image |Ik⟩, and the quantum
image block transformed by the NEQR model |Ik⟩is used as the plaintext |Pk⟩input into
the encryption process.

4 Simulation experiment results and performance analysis
In the simulation experiments of this paper, three groups of simulation experiments were
carried out using Boats graph, Goldhill graph and Man graph respectively, the Boats
and Goldhill graphs are all 512 × 512 and the Man graph is 1024 × 1024. The im-
age dataset was obtained from the public website (https://ccia.ugr.es/cvg/CG/base.htm)
and Github downloads (Github: https://gitcode.com/Premium-Resources/75708.git). The
performance analysis of the simulation results including histograms, correlation, informa-
tion entropy, noise attack, cropping attack, diﬀerential attack, key sensitivity analysis, cor-
relation, information entropy, noise attack, clipping attack, diﬀerential attack and key sen-
sitivity analysis, computational environment for operating the experiments: Windows 10,
64-bit OS, Processor: Intel(R) Core(TM) i7-10750H CPU @ 2.60 GHz, Graphics: NVIDIA
GeForce GTX 1650 Ti (4 GB), Intel(R) UHD Graphics (128 MB).
4.1 Simulation experiment results
The simulation experiment results are shown in Fig. 6. It can be seen intuitively from the
experimental results that the visual information of the original image is eﬀectively hidden,
and no information can be obtained from the encrypted image.
4.2 Histogram and chi-square test analysis
The histogram is a statistical histogram of the distribution of image pixel values. Before
encryption, the histogram of a natural image usually presents a non-uniform distribution,
while an ideal encrypted image should present a nearly uniform histogram distribution.
Histogram analysis of the three images and the encrypted image is performed, and the
experimental results are shown in Fig. 7 and Fig. 8. It can be clearly seen from Fig. 7 that
the histogram of the original image presents a non-uniform distribution, with obvious
peaks and valleys, and is very vulnerable to statistical attacks; while it can be clearly seen
from Fig. 8 that the pixels of the encrypted image are approximately evenly distributed,

4.9 Quantum mechanisms and results analysis
In order to deeply understand the intrinsic correlation between the experimental results
and the algorithm design, this section systematically analyses the root causes of the exper-
imental results in the context of quantum properties and cryptographic architectures.
(1) Quantum basis of statistical homogeneity
Uniform histograms with high entropy values are realised by the superposition inter-
ference eﬀect of alternating quantum random walk. By combining with the image hash
value, the randomness of the key is enhanced, and comparing with the classical chaotic
mechanism, this method circumvents the periodicity of the chaotic system.
(2) Quantum mechanism with low correlation


Song et al. EPJ Quantum Technology           (2025) 12:82 
Page 19 of 20
Neighbouring pixel correlation coeﬃcient close to 0 is achieved by spatial entanglement
destruction in the quantum permutation phase. The SWAP gate employed destroys the
spatial adjacency, and the entanglement leads to indistinguishable pixel positions, and the
original spatial correlation is completely eliminated, resulting in good randomness in pixel
positions.
(3) Architecture design for anti-clipping attack
The large size image anti-clipping attack is achieved by quantum permutation, quan-
tum diﬀusion, and chunking processing together. The quantum permutation stage makes
the cropped region unable to leak local features due to pixel position randomisation; the
quantum diﬀusion stage makes the block-chaining structure to conﬁne the error to a sin-
gle block; and the chunking processing makes each block independently encrypted and
decrypted to avoid the overall collapse.
5 Conclusion
In this paper, a grey-scale image encryption method incorporating quantum features is
proposed based on alternating quantum random walk, which combines random walk and
quantum gates in quantum computing, and is signiﬁcantly innovative in the ﬁeld of im-
age encryption. Through theoretical analysis and simulation experiments, the superiority
of the method in terms of encryption performance and security is veriﬁed. The results
of experimental and simulation analyses show that the quantum encryption scheme pos-
sesses advantages in security that are diﬃcult to be compared with traditional methods,
and improves the encryption strength while ensuring eﬃcient and feasible prospects for
practical applications.
Limitations of this study: this study focuses on grey scale images, but the real-world sce-
narios are mostly colour images and lack of security veriﬁcation against quantum speciﬁc
attacks.
Future work of this study: further research on quantum encryption algorithms for colour
images. Formal validation against quantum attacks using IBM Quantum Attack Toolkit.

Abstract: In recent years, in the context of the rapid development of quantum computing technology, quantum attack methods such as Shor’s algorithm pose a serious threat to the traditional public key encryption system based on number-theoretic puzzles. Using the characteristics of quantum bits, this paper proposes a quantum grey-scale image encryption method based on alternating quantum random walk. Firstly, the quantum representation model is used to transform the image into a quantum state, and then the quantum key is generated by the alternating quantum random walk algorithm, and combined with the quantum gate operation for encrypting the grey-scale image data, which not only inherits the advantage of the anti-attack of the quantum computation, but also, through the quantum parallelism and the non-clonability, which solves the security and eﬃciency bottleneck of traditional image encryption in the quantum era and signiﬁcantly improves the security of grey-scale image encryption. The algorithm proposed in this paper has been veriﬁed by simulation experiments, and the experimental results show that the method is excellent in encryption and decryption eﬀects, and for the encrypted image, a number of performance analyses have been carried out, and the analysis results show that the proposed encryption method has a high degree of security, and it can eﬀectively resist the statistical attack, noise attack, etc., and the distribution of the histogram of encrypted image is more uniform, the pixel correlation analysis is close to 1, and the information entropy is close to 7.999.
